item.title: Your Agent Forgets Every Conversation — mem0's Open-Source Memory Class Gives It Persistent Cross-Session Context in Three Lines
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: mem0's open-source Memory class stores extracted facts per user_id and retrieves them by semantic search — m.add(messages, user_id) then m.search(query, filters) before every LLM call.
item.content:encoded:
**`mem0`'s `Memory` class stores extracted facts per `user_id` and retrieves them by semantic search — `m.add(messages, user_id="alice")` then `m.search(query, filters={"user_id": "alice"})` before every LLM call gives your agent persistent context that survives process restarts.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** write agents that remember user preferences, past decisions, and ongoing project context across separate sessions without building a custom memory system.
- **mem0 extracts facts automatically.** You pass a message list and a `user_id`; mem0 calls an LLM internally (GPT-4.1-nano by default, swappable to Claude or Ollama models via config) to extract memorable facts and stores them in a local Qdrant vector database. - **Search returns ranked memories.** Before each LLM call, search for memories relevant to the current turn; results are short fact strings you inject directly into the system prompt. - **Cross-session by design.** The Qdrant store persists to disk between runs; `Memory()` with no args reconnects to the same store on every instantiation.
**Install and run**
```bash pip install mem0ai ```
```python from mem0 import Memory
m = Memory()
# After the agent replies, store the exchange m.add( messages=[ {"role": "user", "content": "Use PostgreSQL for this project, not MySQL."}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "Noted. I'll use PostgreSQL throughout."}, ], user_id="alice", )
# Before the next LLM call, retrieve relevant memories results = m.search("database choice", filters={"user_id": "alice"}) context = "\n".join(r["memory"] for r in results["results"]) # context: "User prefers PostgreSQL over MySQL." ```
Prepend `context` to the system prompt: `"What you know about this user:\n" + context`.
**Limits**
- Default backends: OpenAI `gpt-4.1-nano` (extraction), `text-embedding-3-small` (vectors), Qdrant (storage), SQLite (history). All swappable — the [configuration docs](https://docs.mem0.ai/open-source/overview) cover Anthropic, Ollama, and pgvector backends. - The open-source version has no rate limits on local runs, but graph memory (entity-relationship graphs across sessions) requires the hosted tier. - Each `add()` call costs one extra LLM call for fact extraction. On short exchanges the overhead is negligible; on long conversations watch latency and cost. - Memory quality depends on the extraction LLM. A cheap default may miss nuanced facts; swap to a more capable model for production use cases where precision matters.
**Sources:** [mem0 open-source Python quickstart — docs.mem0.ai](https://docs.mem0.ai/open-source/python-quickstart) · [Build Long-Term Memory in AI Agents with LangGraph and Mem0 — DigitalOcean / DEV Community](https://dev.to/digitalocean/tutorial-build-long-term-memory-in-ai-agents-with-langgraph-and-mem0-2ln1) · [Mem0 tutorial — datacamp.com](https://www.datacamp.com/tutorial/mem0-tutorial)

item.title: Your Claude Classification Call Returns Text When You Need a Schema — `tool_choice: {type: "tool"}` Eliminates the Maybe
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: Set tool_choice={"type": "tool", "name": "fn"} with a single tool definition and Claude always calls that tool — eliminating the text-vs-tool-call branch from every classification and structured extraction pipeline.
item.content:encoded:
**Define one tool, set `tool_choice={"type": "tool", "name": "fn"}`, and Claude always returns that tool's schema — no text-response fallback, no parsing branch.**
When you add tools to a Claude call with `tool_choice="auto"` (the default), Claude decides whether to call a tool or answer in plain text. That's fine for open-ended agents, but it is the wrong default for classification and structured extraction: your pipeline now has to handle two response shapes, and the plain-text path breaks downstream parsing silently.
**The four `tool_choice` modes:**
```python # auto (default) — Claude decides tool_choice = "auto"
# any — Claude must call some tool tool_choice = "any"
# tool — Claude must call THIS specific tool tool_choice = {"type": "tool", "name": "classify_issue"}
# none — Claude must not call any tool (text only) tool_choice = "none" ```
**Practical example — support ticket classifier:**
```python import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
tools = [{ "name": "classify_issue", "description": "Classify a support ticket", "input_schema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "category": { "type": "string", "enum": ["billing", "technical", "feature_request", "other"] }, "urgency": {"type": "string", "enum": ["low", "medium", "high"]}, "summary": {"type": "string", "maxLength": 120} }, "required": ["category", "urgency", "summary"] } }]
response = client.messages.create( model="claude-haiku-5-5", max_tokens=256, tools=tools, tool_choice={"type": "tool", "name": "classify_issue"}, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Login fails with 500 error after the last deploy."}] )
# Always a tool call — no text-response branch result = response.content[0].input print(result["category"], result["urgency"], result["summary"]) # → technical high Login fails with 500 after last deploy ```
Use `claude-haiku-5-5` for bulk classification — at 1M context and low cost it handles thousands of tickets per hour. Reserve Sonnet for extractions where the reasoning matters.
**Three limits to know:**
1. `tool_choice: {type: "tool"}` and `tool_choice: "any"` are incompatible with extended thinking (`betas=["thinking"]`). You can't force a tool call and get a reasoning trace in the same request. 2. Changing `tool_choice` mid-conversation invalidates the system-prompt cache block. If you have a large system prompt and want caching, pin the same `tool_choice` mode across all turns. 3. `type: "tool"` still requires the named tool to be in the `tools` array — the request errors if the name doesn't match.
**Vs. `client.messages.parse()`:** The Python SDK's `.parse()` method is cleaner if you already control the full call and use Python throughout. `tool_choice` is the right lever when you're building a low-level pipeline, calling from multiple languages, or want to keep the tool schema separately defined.
**Sources:** [Tool use — Anthropic API docs](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/tool-use) · [tool_choice reference — promptlayer.com](https://www.promptlayer.com/glossary/anthropic-tool-choice) · [Claude API best practices 2026 — tkmxai.it.com](https://www.tkmxai.it.com/claude-api-best-practices-checklist-for-production-ai-applications-in-2026)

item.title: Your Embedding Function Calls a Remote API on Every Lookup — sentence-transformers Runs all-MiniLM-L6-v2 Locally in Three Lines
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: sentence-transformers 5.x loads a model from HuggingFace, runs inference locally, and returns 384-dim vectors you can compare with util.semantic_search — no API key, no per-call cost, no rate limit.
item.content:encoded:
**`sentence-transformers` loads `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` locally, embeds your corpus once, and searches it with `util.semantic_search` — no API key, no per-call cost.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:**
- Produce embeddings from any text, entirely offline, with a 40 MB model that fits on a laptop - Understand what the 384-dimensional vector actually is: a fixed position in semantic space where similar sentences land near each other - Run `util.semantic_search` to get ranked hits with cosine scores, ready to pass into a vector store
---
**Install:**
```bash pip install sentence-transformers ```
**Encode a corpus and search it:**
```python from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, util
model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
corpus = [ "How to configure a Postgres connection pool", "Deploying a Python service to Kubernetes", "Setting environment variables in Docker", "Optimizing slow database queries with EXPLAIN", ]
# Encode the corpus once — cache or store these vectors corpus_embeddings = model.encode(corpus, convert_to_tensor=True)
# Encode the query and search query = "How do I pass config to my container?" query_embedding = model.encode(query, convert_to_tensor=True)
hits = util.semantic_search(query_embedding, corpus_embeddings, top_k=2) for hit in hits[0]: print(f"Score: {hit['score']:.3f} | {corpus[hit['corpus_id']]}") ```
Output: ``` Score: 0.512 | Setting environment variables in Docker Score: 0.431 | Deploying a Python service to Kubernetes ```
The query never mentioned Docker — similarity is semantic, not keyword. The model maps both "pass config to my container" and "setting environment variables in Docker" to nearby points in the same 384-dimensional space.
**How it works:** `model.encode()` runs a transformer (a small BERT variant) over each sentence and pools the token embeddings into one fixed-size vector. The model was trained to put sentences with similar meaning close together in cosine distance. That training is what makes the lookup work without any fine-tuning on your data.
**For asymmetric search (short query, long documents):** the standard `encode()` uses a symmetric model. Switch to `multi-qa-mpnet-base-cos-v1` and call `model.encode_query()` / `model.encode_document()` — those apply the model's built-in query and document prompts, which improve retrieval when the two sides look very different in length and style.
**The next step in production:** you wouldn't recompute `corpus_embeddings` on every request. Compute once, save with `numpy.save()` or push the vectors into Qdrant/pgvector, then call your vector store's ANN index instead of `util.semantic_search`. The `util.semantic_search` call above is a brute-force cosine scan — fine for a few hundred documents, slow beyond that.
**Limits:**
- `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` has a 256-token max sequence length. Documents longer than that need chunking before embedding — use `RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter` (covered earlier) and embed each chunk separately. - CPU inference is workable for small corpora but slow at scale. If you're embedding millions of chunks, use a GPU or a hosted embedding API; sentence-transformers ships CUDA support if a GPU is available. - The model is not multilingual. For non-English text use `paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2` (same size, 50+ languages).
**Sources:** [sentence-transformers quickstart — sbert.net](https://sbert.net/docs/quickstart.html) · [Semantic search examples — sbert.net](https://www.sbert.net/examples/applications/semantic-search/README.html) · [all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model card — HuggingFace](https://huggingface.co/sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2)

item.title: REVIEW.md Is How You Tell Claude Code Review What Actually Matters in Your Codebase
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: The GitHub App reads both CLAUDE.md and REVIEW.md. The local /code-review command reads only CLAUDE.md. Knowing that split is how you make PR reviews useful without adding noise to local analysis.
item.content:encoded:
**The Claude Code Review GitHub App reads two files when it reviews a PR: `CLAUDE.md` and `REVIEW.md`. The local `/code-review` command reads only `CLAUDE.md`. Knowing this split is how you make PR reviews useful without adding noise to local analysis.**
`REVIEW.md` is the PR-review-only configuration layer. It sits in your repo root on the default branch and tells the GitHub App what counts as important — without affecting how Claude Code analyzes diffs locally.
**A working REVIEW.md:**
```markdown # Review instructions
## What Important means here Reserve Important for findings that would break behavior, leak data, or block a rollback: incorrect logic, unscoped database queries, PII in logs or error messages, and migrations that aren't backward compatible. Style, naming, and refactoring suggestions are Nit at most.
## Cap the nits Report at most five Nits per review.
## Do not report - Anything CI already enforces: lint, formatting, type errors - Generated files under src/gen/ and any *.lock file - Test-only code that intentionally violates production rules
## Always check - New API routes have an integration test - Log lines don't include email addresses, user IDs, or request bodies - Database queries are scoped to the caller's tenant ```
**Three things REVIEW.md can do that CLAUDE.md cannot:**
1. **Cap the nit count.** "Report at most five Nits per review" applies only to the GitHub App — the local `/code-review` command has no such cap. 2. **Exclude generated files.** Protect `*.lock`, `src/gen/`, or migration files from noise-generating findings. 3. **Add subdirectory rules.** A `backend/REVIEW.md` adds checks specifically for changes under `backend/` — additive to the root file, not a replacement.
**Two things to know before shipping REVIEW.md:**
- **The file is read from the base/default branch, not from the PR.** A `REVIEW.md` added in a PR itself does not take effect — it must already exist on `main` (or your default branch). - **Nit caps and path exclusions require a protected branch.** Without branch protection, the App ignores those directives. Check your branch settings first.
You can also pull in skill files: `@.claude/skills/steward/SKILL.md` loads a per-repo review checklist that both the GitHub App and the babysit/steward system share.
**Sources:** [Customize Claude Code Review — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/code-review-customize)

item.title: Your Claude Agent SDK Has Zero Observability by Default — Three Lines Add Full Traces to Phoenix
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: Every query() call your Claude Agent SDK makes runs in a black box unless you instrument it. Phoenix — Arize's open-source LLM observability platform — adds full span traces in three setup lines.
item.content:encoded:
**Every `query()` call your Claude Agent SDK makes runs in a black box unless you instrument it. Phoenix — Arize's open-source LLM observability platform — adds full span traces in three setup lines.**
Install the OpenInference instrumentation package alongside your SDK:
```bash pip install openinference-instrumentation-claude-agent-sdk claude-agent-sdk arize-phoenix-otel ```
Then, **before any `query()` call**, register Phoenix and let it auto-instrument:
```python from phoenix.otel import register
tracer_provider = register( project_name="my-agent", auto_instrument=True, ) ```
That's it. Every subsequent `query()` call records a span: the model called, tool calls made, token counts, latency, and the full input/output. Open `http://localhost:6006` to browse traces in the Phoenix UI.
**When you need privacy controls** — to hide user inputs or agent outputs from the trace store — skip `auto_instrument` and configure the instrumentor directly:
```python from phoenix.otel import register from openinference.instrumentation.claude_agent_sdk import ClaudeAgentSDKInstrumentor
tracer_provider = register(project_name="my-agent") ClaudeAgentSDKInstrumentor().instrument( tracer_provider=tracer_provider, hide_inputs=True, hide_outputs=True, ) ```
`hide_inputs=True` redacts the messages you send; `hide_outputs=True` redacts model responses. Spans still record timing, tool names, and token counts.
**Three things traces reveal that logs miss:**
1. **Tool call waterfalls** — which tools the agent invoked, in what order, and which ones took the most wall time. 2. **Token spend per task** — how many tokens each `query()` consumed, so you can find expensive paths before they hit your budget. 3. **Failure attribution** — when an agent task fails, the span tree shows whether the problem was in a tool call, a model refusal, or the application layer.
**Limit:** Phoenix stores traces locally by default. For a shared team view or persistence beyond a single dev session, set `PHOENIX_COLLECTOR_ENDPOINT` to point at a hosted Phoenix instance or another OTLP-compatible backend.
**Sources:** [Phoenix × Claude Agent SDK — Arize docs](https://arize.com/docs/phoenix/integrations/python/claude-agent-sdk) · [Claude Agent SDK tracing — Phoenix docs](https://phoenix.arize.com/docs/ax/integrations/python-agent-frameworks/claude-agent-sdk/claude-agent-sdk-tracing.md) · [OpenInference instrumentation — GitHub](https://github.com/Arize-ai/openinference)

item.title: Anthropic's Agents Made 30,000 Commits a Day — Three Patterns That Keep Agent-Driven CI/CD From Imploding
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: Anthropic's engineering post on Scion reveals what happens when agents drive commit volume beyond what git handles. Four patterns that hold up: merge queues, branch-per-task, atomic commits, fast CI.
item.content:encoded:
**Anthropic published the design rationale behind Scion, its in-house VCS that replaced git after agent-generated commits outpaced what git's offline-first architecture could handle. The patterns behind it apply to any agent-driven repo today.**
Git assumes clients work mostly offline with a full copy of the repository. That assumption breaks when most commits come from always-networked agents — CI jobs, coding agents, automated test runners. Secondary coverage of [Anthropic's engineering post](https://anthropic.com/engineering/redesigning-source-control) reports daily merges rising to over 30,000; the post's first design principle for Scion was "clients are always online." Scion itself is internal and not open source — but the workflow patterns it was built to survive are ones you can adopt now.
**Four patterns that hold up at agent commit volume:**
**1. Turn on the merge queue.** GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket all support merge queues. Enable one on any branch where agents push concurrently. Merge queues serialize merges, eliminating the "twenty PRs, all stale from the same branch point" problem that appears the moment parallel agents each open a PR.
**2. One branch per agent task.** Claude Code does this by default via git worktrees. If you're building your own pipeline, give each agent task a fresh branch at task start. Shared feature branches accumulate mid-task conflicts when two tasks run in parallel.
**3. Atomic commits.** Agents shouldn't accumulate 50-file diffs any more than humans should. Keep each commit to one purpose: a CI task that breaks can be reverted cleanly, and a code review tool can reason about a targeted change.
**4. Make CI fast.** At human commit rates, a 10-minute CI run is annoying. At agent commit rates, it becomes a merge-queue bottleneck that backs up indefinitely. Profile the slowest check in your critical path and target under 2 minutes.
**Limit:** These patterns reduce friction; they don't replace a solid test suite. A fast, broken CI is worse than a slow, accurate one.
**Sources:** [Redesigning source control at Anthropic — Anthropic Engineering](https://anthropic.com/engineering/redesigning-source-control) · [Scion coverage with 30k/day figure — fourweekmba.com](https://fourweekmba.com/ai-anthropic-builds-scion-to-replace-git-at-30000-merges-a-day/) · [GitHub merge queues docs](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/configuring-pull-request-merges/managing-a-merge-queue)

item.title: Anthropic's API Version 2026-10-21 Drops temperature, Rejects Document Blocks in Assistant Messages, and Rejects Citation Arrays in User Messages
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: API version 2026-10-21 — first major version since 2023 — removes temperature/top_p/top_k and adds two new 400 rules. Apps on the old version header are unaffected until they migrate.
item.content:encoded:
**Anthropic shipped API version 2026-10-21, the first major API version since 2023-06-01. Three breaking changes trigger 400 errors once you migrate — audit your codebase before upgrading the SDK.**
**The three breaking changes:**
- **Sampling parameters removed.** `temperature`, `top_p`, and `top_k` — including at their previous default values — now return a 400. Omit them entirely. For "deterministic" behavior that you were getting via `temperature=0`, use prompt framing instead ("be precise and consistent"). - **Document blocks in assistant messages rejected.** A `document` block placed directly in an assistant message now returns a 400. Move documents to user messages. Documents inside tool results are still accepted. - **Citation arrays in user message text blocks rejected.** A `text` block in a user message carrying a non-empty `citations` array now returns a 400.
**Migration:** Upgrade the `anthropic` package per [Anthropic's official migration guide](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/migration-2026-10-21), address these three patterns in your codebase, and test before shipping. Apps still sending `anthropic-version: 2023-06-01` continue to work until they adopt the new version.
The temperature restriction was already enforced on Opus 4.7+ models (April 2026). The 2026-10-21 API version formalizes it across all current models and adds the two document and citation rules.
**Why it matters:** Any production integration that passes `temperature` (even `temperature=0`), uses document blocks in assistant turns, or sends citation arrays in user messages will break the moment it upgrades to an SDK that sets the new version header.
**Sources:** [Migration guide — Anthropic Platform Docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/migration-2026-10-21) · [Real-world 400 errors — GitHub: ComfyUI issue](https://github.com/Comfy-Org/ComfyUI/issues/13923) · [Sampling removal coverage — AlphaSignal](https://alphasignal.ai/news/anthropic-rewrites-claude-api-after-3-years-removing-temperature-controls)

item.title: Your LoRA Adapter Runs an Extra Matrix Multiply on Every Inference Call — `merge_and_unload()` Folds It Into the Base Weights
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: After fine-tuning with LoRA or QLoRA, fold the adapter into base weights with merge_and_unload() — one checkpoint, no per-call overhead, no PEFT dependency at serving time.
item.content:encoded:
**After fine-tuning with LoRA or QLoRA, fold the adapter into the base weights with `merge_and_unload()` before deploying — one checkpoint, no adapter overhead, no PEFT dependency at serving time.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Take a LoRA-fine-tuned model from two files (base + adapter) to a single, standard HuggingFace checkpoint you can serve with vLLM, Ollama, or `llama.cpp` without any PEFT dependency at inference.
**Three things to know:** - A LoRA adapter is a pair of low-rank matrices. At inference, every forward pass runs the base layer *plus* the adapter addition. `merge_and_unload()` permanently adds that contribution to the base weights and discards the adapter object. The merged model runs at full base-model speed with no extra computation. - **QLoRA caveat:** if you trained with 4-bit quantization, load the base in `bfloat16` (not `load_in_4bit=True`) before merging. A quantized base cannot be merged directly — the adapter weights are full precision but the base isn't, and the math doesn't compose. - Once merged, you lose the ability to swap or unload the adapter dynamically. If you plan to serve multiple LoRA adapters from one base (e.g., with vLLM's `--enable-lora` flag), keep the original adapter files and skip the merge.
**Walk-through:**
```python from peft import PeftModel from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer import torch
BASE = "meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B" ADAPTER = "your-org/llama-3-1-8b-lora-adapter" # your adapter on HF Hub
# Load base in full precision — 4-bit quantized bases cannot merge base = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( BASE, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto" ) tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(BASE)
# Load adapter on top of base model = PeftModel.from_pretrained(base, ADAPTER)
# Merge adapter weights into the base, drop adapter layers merged = model.merge_and_unload()
# Save as a plain HuggingFace model merged.save_pretrained("./llama-3-1-8b-merged") tokenizer.save_pretrained("./llama-3-1-8b-merged")
# Push to Hub — loads like any standard model, no PEFT needed merged.push_to_hub("your-org/llama-3-1-8b-merged") tokenizer.push_to_hub("your-org/llama-3-1-8b-merged") ```
After pushing, `vllm serve your-org/llama-3-1-8b-merged` and `ollama create` both work without any adapter flags. The serving stack treats it as a standard base model.
**Limit:** merging requires loading the full-precision base, so you need enough VRAM or RAM for the unquantized weights. An 8B model in bfloat16 needs ~16 GB; a 70B model needs ~140 GB (use `device_map="auto"` to offload layers to CPU if needed). The merge itself takes 20–60 seconds on an 8B model. If you need multi-adapter serving (one base, many adapters swapped at runtime), the unmerged path with vLLM's LoRA support is better suited.
**Sources:** [HuggingFace LLM Course — Fine-tuning for deployment (ch. 11)](https://huggingface.co/learn/llm-course/en/chapter11/4), [PEFT LoRA developer guide — merging into base model](https://huggingface.co/docs/peft/main/en/developer_guides/lora#merging-lora-into-the-base-model), [ApX — Merging LoRA adapters with base models (QLoRA precision caveat)](https://apxml.com/courses/fine-tuning-small-language-model/chapter-7-model-merging-and-deployment/merging-lora-adapters-with-base-models)

item.title: Your Parallel Research Subagents Return Walls of Text That Flood the Orchestrator's Context — Have Each Write a Structured File Instead
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: When running 3+ parallel subagents, have each write findings to a structured file; the orchestrator reads selectively at the end, keeping its context clean for synthesis.
item.content:encoded:
**When running parallel research subagents, have each write its findings to a structured file during the run; the orchestrator reads those files once — selectively — instead of receiving all output in context at once.**
Four parallel subagents each returning 3,000 tokens of analysis is 12k tokens in the parent's context window before synthesis starts. The most important details are buried between the boilerplate, and you've spent a meaningful share of your context budget on raw delivery.
**The pattern: instruct each subagent to write its output to a file**
In the prompt for each parallel `Agent()` call, specify a file path and a structured format:
``` Investigate the authentication flow in the codebase and write your findings to .claude/research/auth.md. Use this exact structure:
## Summary (3 sentences max) ## Key files (paths only) ## Issues found (bulleted list) ## Recommendation (1 sentence)
Do not return the full analysis in your reply — write it to the file and confirm the path when done. ```
Run all subagents in a single response (multiple `Agent()` calls so they execute in parallel). Once they complete, read only what you need:
``` Read the ## Issues found sections from .claude/research/auth.md, .claude/research/payments.md, and .claude/research/sessions.md. Rank every issue by severity and produce a prioritized fix plan. ```
The orchestrator's context now holds one targeted synthesis read instead of three full reports.
**Why it works:** Claude Code subagents write files by default (same permission scope as the orchestrator unless restricted). The file lives outside the context window until you choose to read it — and you can read only the section you need. The parent session stays uncluttered for the synthesis step where careful reasoning actually matters.
**When to keep in-context output:** read-only subagents you've scoped with `permissions: { allowed_tools: [Read, Grep, Glob] }` shouldn't be writing files — keep them limited and constrain their reply instead (ask for a 5-bullet summary). The file pattern also doesn't help for sequential chains where each step's output is the next step's input: there, the dependency is real and you're not fighting context bloat, you're building on it.
**Limit:** `.claude/research/` is a reasonable project-local path, but it will be staged if you do a broad `git add`. Use a `.gitignore` entry or write to a temp dir when the findings are ephemeral. Temp files (`/tmp/`) disappear across sessions, so write to the project directory for anything you'll need in a follow-up session.
**Sources:** [Claude Code agent SDK — subagents](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents), [LangGraph state persistence](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/concepts/persistence/) (the same write-intermediate-results-to-storage principle in a multi-agent framework)

item.title: Your Embedding Pipeline Handles Text Only — EmbeddingGemma 2 Puts Text, Images, and Audio Into One 768-Dim Space Locally
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: EmbeddingGemma 2 (Google, Apache 2.0, 740M params, Oct 6) maps text, images, and audio into one 768-dim vector space — one local model for multimodal RAG, no separate encoders per modality.
item.content:encoded:
**EmbeddingGemma 2 (Google, Apache 2.0, 740M params) maps text, code, images, and audio into a single 768-dimensional embedding space — one locally-runnable model for multimodal RAG without separate encoders per modality.**
Most RAG pipelines are text-only: embed documents, embed queries, compare vectors. When your corpus mixes screenshots, product images, or audio recordings with text, you typically need separate embedding models for each modality — or you transcribe and describe everything into text first, losing fidelity.
EmbeddingGemma 2 changes that. Its core is a 270M text encoder; a vision encoder and audio encoder attach only when you pass non-text inputs. All modalities project into the same 768-dim space, so an image query returns text documents and vice versa.
**Get started:**
```bash pip install transformers accelerate ```
```python from transformers import AutoModel, AutoProcessor import torch
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("google/embeddinggemma-2", trust_remote_code=True) processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained("google/embeddinggemma-2")
# Embed text inputs = processor(text="What is speculative decoding?", return_tensors="pt") text_emb = model(**inputs).last_hidden_state.mean(dim=1)
# Embed an image (PIL Image) from PIL import Image img = Image.open("diagram.png") inputs = processor(images=img, return_tensors="pt") image_emb = model(**inputs).last_hidden_state.mean(dim=1)
# Cosine similarity works directly across modalities import torch.nn.functional as F score = F.cosine_similarity(text_emb, image_emb) ```
Both return `[1, 768]` float tensors. Cross-modal cosine similarity works because both modalities share the same projection head.
**Matryoshka truncation:** slice the output to 512, 256, or 128 dims if your vector store has a fixed dimension or you're optimizing index size. The model is trained with Matryoshka Representation Learning, so shorter slices still preserve relative ordering.
**When to reach for it:** - Corpus mixes images, diagrams, or audio with text (product catalogs, design docs, recorded meetings) - You want a single local model rather than a cloud vision API per document
**When to skip it:** - Text-only workloads: at 740M params it is roughly 30× larger than `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` (22M) for no gain on text-only inputs — use a smaller dedicated model - Google reports an 8K-token context window; that figure has not been independently confirmed - Per-modality accuracy benchmarks from independent sources are not yet published; Google's own eval results have not been replicated in peer-reviewed settings
**Sources:** [EmbeddingGemma 2 model overview — Google AI for Developers](https://ai.google.dev/gemma/docs/embeddinggemma) · [Why Google's Small EmbeddingGemma 2 Deserves More Attention — Towards AI](https://pub.towardsai.net/why-googles-small-embeddinggemma-2-model-deserves-more-attention-9d127ae57697) · [EmbeddingGemma 2: Google's tiny AI model for multimodal search — YourStory](https://yourstory.com/ai-story/embeddinggemma-2-google-tiny-ai-multimodal-search) · [google/embeddinggemma-2 — Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/google/embeddinggemma-2)

item.title: Your vLLM Server Generates One Token at a Time — EAGLE3 Speculative Decoding Drafts Tokens Ahead and Verifies in a Single Forward Pass
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: Add --speculative-config to vllm serve with an EAGLE3 draft checkpoint to propose several tokens ahead; the target verifies in one parallel forward pass with zero quality loss.
item.content:encoded:
**Add `--speculative-config '{"method":"eagle3","model":"<draft>","num_speculative_tokens":3}'` to `vllm serve` to cut token-generation latency using a lightweight draft model — output quality is mathematically identical to running the target alone.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** - Enable EAGLE3 speculative decoding on any vLLM-served model that has a published draft checkpoint - Set `num_speculative_tokens` for your workload and measure the acceptance rate before committing - Understand when speculative decoding helps (long-context, chat-like prompts) vs. when it slows you down (short, dissimilar prompts)
## How it works
Standard autoregressive generation calls the full target model once per output token. Speculative decoding uses a cheaper *draft* model to propose *k* tokens ahead, then calls the target once to verify all *k* in parallel. If the target agrees, you've paid one forward pass for *k* tokens instead of *k* passes. When it rejects a draft token, it falls back to the target's correct token — so output distribution is identical to the un-speculated target.
EAGLE3 conditions the draft model on the target's hidden states (rather than just the output logits), which gives higher acceptance rates on instruction-tuned models than earlier EAGLE versions.
## Step-by-step
**1. Find a compatible draft checkpoint**
The draft and target must share the same model family and architecture. Red Hat publishes EAGLE3 checkpoints for Llama 3.1 8B on Hugging Face:
``` red-hat-research/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-EAGLE3 ```
Browse the `eagle3-checkpoints` Hugging Face organization for other families.
**2. Serve with `--speculative-config`**
```bash vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct --speculative-config '{ "method": "eagle3", "model": "red-hat-research/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-EAGLE3", "num_speculative_tokens": 3, "draft_tensor_parallel_size": 1 }' ```
`draft_tensor_parallel_size` must be `1` for EAGLE3 even if your target uses tensor parallelism.
**3. Benchmark before committing**
Run the same prompt batch with and without the flag. AMD reports up to 2.3× throughput on Llama 3.1 70B with a 1B draft on ROCm hardware — that figure is AMD's own benchmark on AMD hardware and varies significantly by prompt length, batch size, and workload type. On coding tasks with long system prompts, acceptance rates tend to be higher than on diverse chat tasks.
Check vLLM's logs for `draft_acceptance_rate`. If it falls below ~0.5, the draft isn't well-aligned with your workload and you may see a slowdown rather than a speedup.
## Limits
- Draft and target must share the same model family — you cannot use a Mistral draft for a Llama target - `num_speculative_tokens` too high → acceptance rate drops; too low → overhead outweighs gains. Start at 3 and tune with your actual prompt distribution - The `method: ngram` alternative requires no draft model but only helps on repetitive prompts (code with boilerplate, templated output) - EAGLE3 draft checkpoints for newer model families (Llama 4, Gemma 4) are sparse — check the `eagle3-checkpoints` organization on Hugging Face before expecting coverage - `draft_tensor_parallel_size: 1` means the draft model loads on a single GPU; on multi-GPU setups this can create a memory imbalance if the draft is large
**Sources:** [Speculative Decoding in vLLM — vLLM docs](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/features/spec_decode.html) · [Deploy EAGLE3 speculative decoding with vLLM Neuron — AWS Neuron](https://awsdocs-neuron.readthedocs-hosted.com/en/latest/vllm-neuron/docs/tutorials/tutorial-eagle3-speculative-decoding-llama-3-1.html) · [Speculative Decoding Deep Dive (AMD ROCm, Llama 3.1 70B benchmark)](https://rocm.docs.amd.com/projects/ai-developer-hub/en/v9.0/notebooks/inference/speculative_decoding_deep_dive.html) · [vLLM Speculators project guide](https://docs.vllm.ai/projects/speculators/en/latest/user_guide/tutorials/serve_vllm/)

item.title: Claude Code's Read Tool Truncates Large Files at a Fixed Cap — `allow_large: true` Reads Them Whole When the Session Has Context Room
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: Claude Code v2.1.296 added allow_large: true to the Read tool. When context has room, Claude reads a text file whole instead of chunking at the ~25K token default cap — the read is sized against remaining session context.
item.content:encoded:
**Claude Code v2.1.296 added `allow_large: true` to the Read tool — when the session has context room, Claude reads a text file whole in one call instead of chunking it across multiple offset/limit reads.**
The Read tool has a default size cap: roughly 25,000 tokens in the CLI and 10,000 in Claude Desktop. Before v2.1.296 (October 9, 2026), a file that exceeded the cap would require multiple chunk reads with `offset` and `limit` — Claude would have to stitch the results, sometimes losing inter-section relationships in the process.
`allow_large: true` removes the cap and instead sizes the read against whatever context space the session has at call time. Claude sets the parameter itself based on current session budget; there is no user-facing flag to force it.
**What this means for how you structure sessions:**
- **Start large-file tasks fresh.** If your task is a deep audit of a 20,000-line generated file, open a new session or run `/compact` early. A full read late in a busy session still falls back to chunks because the context has less room. - **Subagent sessions start empty.** An Agent tool call or forked subagent inherits nothing from the orchestrator's session — so it can read a large file whole even when the parent session is half full. Structure analysis of large files as a subagent if the orchestrator conversation is already deep. - **Explicit `limit` still wins.** `allow_large` affects the automatic cap, not a `limit` you set explicitly. Passing `limit: 500` still reads 500 lines even if the file is small.
**Limits:** Claude sets the parameter itself; the behavior is not user-configurable. The exact behavior is not yet fully documented in the official tools reference as of October 2026 — check [code.claude.com/docs](https://code.claude.com/docs) before relying on it in production. Applies to text files; images, PDFs, and Jupyter notebooks follow separate size rules and are not affected.
**Sources:** [Claude Code v2.1.296 Major Updates: autoCompactWindow and allow_large — dev.classmethod.jp](https://dev.classmethod.jp/en/articles/20261010-cc-updates-v2-1-296/) · [Claude Code File Size Limits and Large File Handling — fast.io](https://fast.io/resources/claude-code-file-size-limit/)

item.title: Your Query Embeds From One Angle — LangChain's `MultiQueryRetriever` Generates Variants, Retrieves for Each, and Returns the Unique Union
item.dc:creator: Claude Code Tree
item.description: MultiQueryRetriever asks an LLM to rewrite your query from 3+ angles, runs each against the same vector store, and deduplicates the combined results — better recall without re-chunking or re-indexing.
item.content:encoded:
**What you'll be able to do after this:** expand vector search recall without re-chunking or re-indexing by rewriting the query from multiple angles before the search runs.
Vector similarity is path-dependent. "Show me revenue trends" and "quarterly income graphs" embed differently and can return different chunks from the same index — even when those chunks are directly relevant to both phrasings. A retriever that only runs your original query misses chunks that align with a slightly different framing.
`MultiQueryRetriever` addresses this: it passes your question to an LLM, asks it to generate three rephrased variants, retrieves documents for each variant, and returns the deduplicated union. Your vector store and chunks stay untouched.
**Three takeaways:** 1. The LLM generates variants at `temperature=0` by default — deterministic reformulations, not creative ones. The goal is angle coverage, not novelty. 2. Deduplication is by document identity: a chunk that surfaces in two variant results appears once in the final set. 3. One extra LLM call per user query. Size it with a fast, cheap model — the variants it writes are short prompts, not complex reasoning tasks.
**How to wire it in:**
```python from langchain_community.vectorstores import Chroma from langchain_anthropic import ChatAnthropic from langchain_openai import OpenAIEmbeddings from langchain.retrievers.multi_query import MultiQueryRetriever
vectordb = Chroma( persist_directory="./my_chroma_db", embedding_function=OpenAIEmbeddings() ) base_retriever = vectordb.as_retriever(search_kwargs={"k": 5})
# Any fast, cheap model works for variant generation llm = ChatAnthropic(model="claude-haiku-5-5", temperature=0)
retriever = MultiQueryRetriever.from_llm( retriever=base_retriever, llm=llm, include_original=True, # adds your original query to the variant set )
docs = retriever.invoke("What are the latency implications of adding a reranker?") ```
To inspect the variants it generated:
```python import logging logging.getLogger("langchain.retrievers.multi_query").setLevel(logging.INFO) ```
**Limits:** - Adds one LLM call and extra vector queries per user request — latency compounds if `k` is large or the vector store is slow - Recall gain diminishes past 5–7 variants; the default 3 is a reasonable starting point - Over-retrieves on narrow factual lookups where the original query is already precise; for those, a plain retriever is faster and sufficient

Each agent restarts from scratch because there's no authoritative source for "never `npm install`, always `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`" or "run `typecheck` before committing, not just `tsc`."
AGENTS.md is that file. It's a plain Markdown file at your repository root that any conformant coding agent reads before acting. It's an AAIF standard (Linux Foundation, since December 2025), so the same file reaches every tool that implements it — not just Claude Code.

item.title: Your SFT Model Gets the Task Right But Responds in the Wrong Tone — DPO Aligns Style Without a Reward Model
item.author: Claude Code Tree
item.description: DPO replaces RLHF's reward model and PPO loop with a single classifier loss on (prompt, chosen, rejected) triplets — same TRL install you use for SFT, runs on one GPU with a small preference dataset.
item.content:encoded:
**DPO replaces RLHF's reward model and PPO loop with a single classifier loss on (prompt, chosen, rejected) triplets — same TRL install you already use for SFT, runs on one GPU with a small preference dataset.**
SFT teaches a model what to do. After fine-tuning on your task data, it answers correctly — but in a style that doesn't match your use case: too verbose, too casual, too blunt. That is a behavior gap, not a knowledge gap, and SFT alone can't close it.
Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) aligns behavioral style from a preference dataset. Traditional RLHF requires a separate reward model and a PPO training loop — expensive, unstable, and complex to tune. DPO absorbs the reward signal directly into the language model loss on `{prompt, chosen, rejected}` triplets. The loss increases the probability of the chosen response and decreases the rejected one, relative to a frozen reference (your SFT base). No reward model. No PPO. One `.train()` call.
**What you'll be able to do after this:** fine-tune a model's behavioral style — tone, verbosity, format, safety refusals — on top of a task-trained SFT base, using TRL's DPOTrainer and a small preference dataset.
**Three things to know before you start:** 1. **SFT first, DPO second.** DPO requires a strong task-trained base. Running it on an instruction-naive model produces unstable gradients. 2. **Your dataset is `{prompt, chosen, rejected}` pairs.** One prompt, two responses: one preferred, one dispreferred. `trl-lib/ultrafeedback_binarized` is the canonical public example; for domain-specific alignment, generate pairs with an LLM judge comparing two generations. 3. **`beta` controls the leash.** Lower beta (0.05) lets the model diverge further from the SFT base; higher beta (0.5) keeps it close. Start at 0.1 and tune from there.
## Walk-through
```bash pip install trl transformers datasets ```
```python from datasets import load_dataset from trl import DPOConfig, DPOTrainer from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("your-sft-checkpoint", torch_dtype="auto") tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("your-sft-checkpoint")
# Dataset must have "prompt", "chosen", "rejected" columns dataset = load_dataset("trl-lib/ultrafeedback_binarized", split="train[:2000]")
training_args = DPOConfig( output_dir="dpo-output", num_train_epochs=1, per_device_train_batch_size=2, beta=0.1, ) trainer = DPOTrainer( model=model, args=training_args, processing_class=tokenizer, # note: `tokenizer=` arg is deprecated in TRL v1.x train_dataset=dataset, ) trainer.train() ```
DPOTrainer uses your loaded model as both the trained model and the reference policy (frozen copy). It handles tokenization, loss computation, and logging without additional setup.
## Limits
A high `beta` makes DPO converge toward the SFT base and the style signal washes out; a very low `beta` can destabilize training. Building quality preference pairs is the hard part: synthetic LLM-judged pairs introduce label noise proportional to how closely the judge's preferences match yours. For small style shifts, 500–2,000 pairs is often enough. For safety-critical alignment, you need human-rated pairs and a much larger dataset. DPO does not improve task accuracy — if the base model makes factual errors, DPO won't fix them.
**Sources:** [TRL DPOTrainer docs](https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/main/en/dpo_trainer) · [Maxime Labonne's DPO Colab — TRL community tutorials](https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/en/community_tutorials) · [Rafailov et al., "Direct Preference Optimization" (arXiv:2305.18290)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290) · [IBM Skills Network DPO guided project](https://catalog.skills.network/catalog_item/6413)

item.author: Claude Code Tree

item.content:encoded:
Anthropic's beta User Profiles API (released Oct 20, 2026) lets you attach a stable per-customer identity to every Claude API call. You get per-user dashboards, spend limits, and rate-limit budgets without building your own metering layer.
**What you'll be able to do after this:** route multi-tenant API calls through named user profiles so Anthropic's dashboard breaks out cost and usage by customer, and enforce per-customer token budgets, with about ten lines of code.

```python import anthropic client = anthropic.Anthropic()
# Create a profile for a customer (idempotent by external_user_id) profile = client.beta.user_profiles.create( external_user_id="customer-42", name="Acme Corp", access_type="application" # "passthrough" for resellers )
# Attach the profile to every call for this customer message = client.messages.create( model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=1024, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}], extra_headers={"anthropic-user-profile-id": profile.id} ) ```
`access_type="application"` means you're calling on behalf of your own product. `"passthrough"` is for platforms that resell API access directly — it requires Anthropic approval.

Once a profile ID appears in requests, the Anthropic console shows: - Token usage broken out by profile - Spend over time per customer - Rate-limit headroom per profile (set via the API)

item.content:encoded:
Anthropic announced on Oct 22, 2026 that it is donating the **Agent Skills** specification to the **AI Alliance and Interoperability Forum (AAIF)**, the Linux Foundation body that already stewards MCP. According to Anthropic, the Skills ecosystem now counts 70+ integrated platforms, ~1 M published skills, and 280 M cumulative installs.
## What Agent Skills is
Agent Skills is a standard that lets users bundle a reusable capability — a prompt template, a tool binding, a short agentic workflow — into a shareable artifact that any compliant agent host can discover and invoke. Think of it as the package-manager layer on top of MCP's protocol layer: MCP defines how an agent calls a tool; Skills defines how you package and distribute a named, versioned capability that wraps those calls.
## Why the AAIF donation matters
Handing the spec to the Linux Foundation removes Anthropic as sole steward and opens governance to the broader ecosystem. The AAIF already governs MCP this way. Together the two donations mean both the transport (MCP) and the packaging (Skills) layers of agent interoperability live in neutral hands — a prerequisite for enterprise procurement teams that need vendor-independence assurances.
SDTimes covered the AAIF's formation when MCP was donated in late 2025: the body was explicitly designed as a home for agent-interoperability standards across vendors.
## The limit: integrated ≠ interoperable
70 platforms list Skills support, but "support" ranges from native invocation to a compatibility shim. A skill authored for Claude Code may need manual porting to work in a different agent host. The spec defines the format, not the runtime semantics — until conformance tests are published and vendors certify against them, interoperability is best-effort.
**Source:** Anthropic, "Agent Skills" announcement (Oct 22, 2026) — [anthropic.com/news/agent-skills](https://www.anthropic.com/news/agent-skills); AAIF background — SD Times coverage of the Linux Foundation AI body (Dec 2025). *Note: as of Oct 23, 2026 the specific Oct 22 donation announcement has not yet appeared in independent tech-outlet news cycles; the AAIF governance context and the 70+/1 M/280 M figures are Anthropic's own.*

item.title: LangChain @before_model: Trim Context Windows Before They Overflow Your Agent
item.author: Claude Code Tree
item.description: After 40+ agent turns the message list overflows. LangChain's @before_model decorator and trim_messages utility let you trim older messages before every LLM call — no call-site changes required.
item.content:encoded:
Long-running agents quietly hit their context limit one message at a time. When the list finally overflows you get a truncation error or a mysteriously wrong answer — neither is obvious. LangChain's `@before_model` decorator and `trim_messages` utility let you enforce a context budget before every LLM call, with no changes to the rest of your graph.
**Curriculum area:** Applied/agentic → Memory & context engineering.
## The problem
Every turn in a LangGraph agent appends to `state["messages"]`. After 40–50 turns on a long conversation — or a few turns with large tool outputs — the accumulated history blows past the model's context window. The model silently truncates or the API returns a 400. Neither tells you which messages were lost.
## Two strategies with one decorator
`@before_model` is middleware that intercepts `state` before the LLM call. Return a modified state and LangChain uses that for the call — original state is unchanged.
```python from langchain_core.messages import trim_messages from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, MessagesState
# Strategy 1 — count-based: keep system message + last 20 messages def keep_last_20(state): msgs = state["messages"] # Always preserve the system message at index 0 return {"messages": [msgs[0]] + msgs[-20:] if len(msgs) > 21 else msgs}
# Strategy 2 — token-based: keep system message + last 4,000 tokens def trim_by_tokens(state): return { "messages": trim_messages( state["messages"], max_tokens=4_000, strategy="last", token_counter=len, # swap for a real tokenizer in production include_system=True, allow_partial=False, # never split a message mid-sentence ) } ```
Wire it in when you build the graph:
```python from langgraph.prebuilt import create_react_agent
agent = create_react_agent( model=llm, tools=tools, pre_model_hook=keep_last_20, # or trim_by_tokens ) ```
## Choosing a strategy
| | Count-based | Token-based | |---|---|---| | **Predictable** | Yes — always exactly N messages | No — depends on message length | | **Accurate** | No — a long tool output costs 10× a short one | Yes | | **Cost** | Cheap | Requires a tokenizer call per turn |
For most agents, start with count-based (simple, no tokenizer dependency). Upgrade to token-based once you know your tool outputs vary widely in length.
## What trim_messages does not do
- It does not summarize dropped messages. If your agent needs to recall facts from turn 5 while operating at turn 50, dropping those messages silently corrupts behavior. Add a summarization step before dropping (see LangGraph's "add summary of conversation history" how-to). - `token_counter=len` counts characters, not tokens — fast for development, wrong for production. Swap in `model.get_num_tokens_from_messages(msgs)` or a tiktoken call. - `allow_partial=False` means a single oversized message is never split — if one tool output exceeds `max_tokens` on its own, trim_messages raises. Handle this upstream by truncating tool outputs before they enter state.
**Sources:** LangGraph "How to add summary of the conversation history" — [langchain-ai.github.io](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/how-tos/memory/add-summary-of-the-conversation-history/); LangChain Core `trim_messages` reference — [python.langchain.com](https://python.langchain.com/docs/how_to/trim_messages/); LangGraph prebuilt `create_react_agent` + `pre_model_hook` — [langchain-ai.github.io](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/reference/prebuilt/).
**Limits:** `token_counter=len` counts characters, not tokens — replace with a real tokenizer before shipping; `trim_messages` does not summarize dropped history; `allow_partial=False` will raise on a single message that exceeds `max_tokens`.

item.title: Your CLAUDE.md Grows Into a Context Sink — Anthropic's Guide Defines When to Use a Skill, Hook, or Subagent Instead
item.author: Claude Code Tree
item.description: Every line in CLAUDE.md loads every turn and costs context. Anthropic's June 2026 guide defines when to use a skill, hook, or subagent instead.
item.content:encoded:
Every line in CLAUDE.md loads every turn and costs context. Anthropic's June 2026 "Steering Claude Code" guide names four mechanisms and tells you when to reach for each one.
**What you'll be able to do after this:** stop packing every constraint into one growing markdown file and instead route each concern to the mechanism that handles it best.
## The four mechanisms
| Mechanism | When it loads | Use for | |---|---|---| | **CLAUDE.md** | Every turn, always | Persistent project context: repo layout, style rules, required preambles, non-negotiable invariants | | **Skill** | Only when invoked by name | Specialized multi-step workflows: publishing a post, running a deploy, scaffolding a feature | | **Hook** | On every matching tool event, outside the context window | Enforcement that must run regardless of prompt state: secret scanning, schema validation, lint-on-save | | **Subagent** | Spawned explicitly, isolated context window | Parallel research, long-running tasks, work whose tool noise you don't want back in the main thread |
## When the lines blur
A constraint that must fire without being asked is a hook, not a CLAUDE.md rule — hooks run outside the model's context so they cannot be reasoned around.
A workflow you invoke by name (`/publish-post`, `/deploy-staging`) is a skill, not a CLAUDE.md section — skills load only when called and can include their own tools and sub-steps.
Parallel or context-expensive work belongs in a subagent — forking keeps the main thread clean and lets several tasks finish at once.
CLAUDE.md stays for the rest: the standing facts every turn needs.
## In practice
Start pruning when CLAUDE.md passes ~200 lines. For each block ask: does this need to be present in every single turn? If it fires only on an event → hook. If it runs only on explicit invocation → skill. If it's parallel or noisy → subagent. The remainder is genuine CLAUDE.md material.
**Source:** Anthropic, "Steering Claude Code: Skills, Hooks, Rules, Subagents, and More" (June 18, 2026) — [claude.com/blog](https://claude.com/blog/steering-claude-code-skills-hooks-rules-subagents-and-more); hooks reference — [docs.anthropic.com](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code/hooks); independent analysis — [Towards AI](https://pub.towardsai.net/claude-code-skills-vs-subagents-vs-hooks-vs-workflows-which-to-use-in-2026-120db6ae5b3c).
**Limits:** Skill invocation depends on description clarity — a vague description causes Claude to miss the skill entirely. Hooks add ~500 ms round-trip latency per matched tool call; keep hook scripts fast.

item.title: Your Open Model Returns Free-Form Text When You Need JSON — vLLM's GuidedDecodingParams Constrains Any Model to a Schema at the Decoding Level
item.author: Claude Code Tree
item.description: Pass a Pydantic schema to GuidedDecodingParams and vLLM guarantees valid JSON from any open model — the constraint operates at token selection, not prompt engineering.
item.content:encoded:
**What you'll be able to do after this:** configure any vLLM-served open model to return valid, schema-conforming JSON on every call — without prompt tricks, retry loops, or post-processing parsers.
## Why prompt engineering alone isn't enough
Asking a model to "respond in JSON" works until it doesn't — a missed bracket, an extra key, a value in the wrong type. For production pipelines that parse the output programmatically, "usually correct" is not acceptable.
vLLM's `GuidedDecodingParams` solves this at the token level. Instead of constraining the prompt, it constrains the sampling step: at each token position, only tokens that keep the output on a valid path through the schema's finite-state automaton are eligible. The model cannot produce invalid JSON even if the instructions say nothing about format.
## Minimal working example
```python from typing import Literal from pydantic import BaseModel from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams from vllm.sampling_params import GuidedDecodingParams
class Review(BaseModel): sentiment: Literal["positive", "negative", "neutral"] score: float # 0.0–1.0 summary: str
llm = LLM(model="mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3") params = SamplingParams( temperature=0, guided_decoding=GuidedDecodingParams(json=Review.model_json_schema()), ) outputs = llm.generate( ["Review: 'Excellent build quality, but battery life is poor.'"], params, ) result = Review.model_validate_json(outputs[0].outputs[0].text) # result.sentiment == "negative", result.score == 0.35, result.summary == "..." ```
`GuidedDecodingParams` accepts `json` (a JSON Schema dict), `regex` (a pattern), `choice` (a list of strings), or `grammar` (a BNF/EBNF string). Pydantic's `.model_json_schema()` gives you the dict directly.
## Three things to know
- **It's a sampling constraint, not a prompt constraint.** The model still uses the prompt for meaning; only the token selection step is restricted. - **xgrammar is the default backend** (as of vLLM 0.6+). It compiles the schema to a pushdown automaton once per schema shape and reuses it across requests. - **Batch inference works.** Pass a list of prompts to `llm.generate()` with the same `params`; each output is independently constrained.
## Limits
xgrammar doesn't support every JSON Schema feature: `$ref` cycles, `allOf` with incompatible types, and some `if/then/else` constructs are unsupported. There is a per-schema compilation cost on first use (~10–50 ms depending on schema complexity); subsequent requests with the same schema pay nothing. Very large or recursive schemas can slow the sampler.
**Sources:** [vLLM Structured Outputs docs](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/features/structured_outputs.html); [Guided Decoding in RAG — arXiv 2509.06631](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.06631v1); [vLLM community forum — guided decoding speed tips, July 2026](https://discuss.vllm.ai/t/as-of-july-2026-what-are-some-general-tips-in-improving-the-speed-of-guided-decoding-in-vllm/2845).

item.title: Your RAG Pipeline Splits Documents at Arbitrary Byte Boundaries — RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter Falls Back Through Paragraph, Line, and Word Separators to Keep Context Together
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter splits on paragraph breaks first, then lines, then spaces — never at a random byte offset — keeping context units intact before they are embedded.
item.content:encoded:
**RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter splits on paragraph breaks first, then lines, then spaces — so chunks respect sentence and paragraph boundaries rather than landing mid-sentence inside your vector store.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** - Split any text document into context-preserving chunks ready for embedding - Choose chunk_size and chunk_overlap values that match your embedding model and retrieval setup - Know when to swap for a structure-aware splitter instead
## Why the splitter choice matters
A fixed-size character split at byte offset 512 cuts sentences mid-thought. The embedded fragment loses its subject. Your retriever then surfaces partial answers as the best match.
`RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter` avoids this by trying a cascade of separators in order — paragraph breaks (`
`), then line breaks (` `), then spaces (` `), then individual characters as a last resort. It only falls to a finer separator when a chunk still exceeds `chunk_size` after splitting on the coarser one.
## Minimal setup
```python pip install langchain-text-splitters ```
```python from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter
splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter( chunk_size=500, # max characters per chunk chunk_overlap=50, # characters re-used from the end of the prior chunk length_function=len, # default; swap for tiktoken to count tokens instead )
# Split plain text chunks = splitter.split_text(your_long_string)
# Split LangChain Document objects (keeps .metadata: source, page, etc.) from langchain_community.document_loaders import TextLoader docs = TextLoader("README.md").load() doc_chunks = splitter.split_documents(docs) ```
`split_documents` preserves `metadata` from the loader — `source`, `page`, and any custom keys — so each chunk knows where it came from.
## Sizing decisions
| Document type | chunk_size (chars) | chunk_overlap | |---|---|---| | Prose / articles | 400–600 | 50–80 | | FAQ / short paragraphs | 150–300 | 30–50 | | Code (use `language=` variant) | 1000–2000 | 200 |
Start at 500/50 and measure retrieval recall on your own data before optimising. Most embedding models have a 512-token limit; 500 characters is roughly 375–400 tokens for English prose, which leaves safe margin.
**Counting tokens instead of characters:**
```python import tiktoken enc = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base") # matches OpenAI & many open models
splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter( chunk_size=400, # now in tokens, not characters chunk_overlap=40, length_function=lambda text: len(enc.encode(text)), ) ```
## When to reach for a different splitter
`RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter` does not know what a heading, table, code fence, or list item is — it splits on whitespace patterns only. Two situations where it causes problems:
- **Markdown with headers**: use `MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter` to split by `#` / `##` / `###` levels. Each chunk then carries the header path as metadata, which lets you filter by section at retrieval time. - **PDFs and structured documents**: use Docling's `DOC_CHUNKS` mode (covered in an [earlier post](https://cloudcodetree.com/ai-news/2026-10-14-03-docling-langchain-pdf-table-structure-rag)). Docling preserves table rows and section breaks before the chunks reach LangChain.
**Limits:** `chunk_overlap` is a *target*, not a guarantee — if the final separator that fits a chunk is longer than the overlap window, the actual overlap may be zero for that pair. And character-based sizing means two chunks with identical character counts can have very different token counts depending on vocabulary (code, URLs, and numbers are cheap in characters but expensive in tokens). Measure before you deploy.

item.title: Your Python Automation Script Ships Without Its Own Requirements — PEP 723 Puts the Dependencies Inside the File; `uv run script.py` Installs Them and Runs
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: PEP 723 lets you declare pip dependencies in a comment block at the top of any .py file. `uv run script.py` reads the block, builds a temp venv, and runs — one command, no setup.
item.content:encoded:
**PEP 723 embeds pip dependencies directly in a `.py` file as a comment block. `uv run script.py` reads the block, builds a temporary virtual environment, and executes — no requirements.txt, no Makefile step, no `pip install` before the script runs.**
This matters for automation scripts you write alongside Claude Code tasks, share via a repo, or run in CI: the script is the whole package. Drop it in your `.claude/hooks/` directory, check it into the repo, and any machine with `uv` installed runs it correctly from the first `uv run`.
## The inline dependency block (PEP 723)
```python # /// script # requires-python = ">=3.11" # dependencies = [ # "httpx", # "rich>=13.0", # ] # ///
import httpx from rich import print
r = httpx.get("https://api.example.com/status") print(r.json()) ```
The `# /// script` block is parsed by uv before execution. Everything between `# ///` and the closing `# ///` is TOML. `dependencies` is a list of PEP 508 dependency specifiers — the same format as requirements.txt.
## Three commands you'll use daily
```bash # Scaffold a new self-contained script uv init --script analyze.py --python 3.12
# Add a dependency — writes it into the block in-place uv add --script analyze.py httpx
# Run without activating anything uv run analyze.py ```
`uv add --script` adds the dependency and updates the inline block atomically; there is no separate file to keep in sync.
## In CI (GitHub Actions)
```yaml - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v3 - run: uv run scripts/validate.py ```
No `pip install` step, no requirements cache to maintain. uv installs the declared deps to an ephemeral environment that it caches across CI runs by content hash.
## Claude Code angle
Claude Code uses `uv` internally for its own Python tool calls. Hooks written as uv scripts match that toolchain exactly — `uv run` in a `PreToolUse` or `PostToolUse` hook works consistently across local machines and cloud sessions without a system Python or an activated venv.
## Limits
- Only uv reads PEP 723 natively — running the script with `python script.py` skips the block and fails with an import error. The `#!/usr/bin/env -S uv run --script` shebang makes the file self-executing on Unix if uv is on PATH. - `uv add --script` writes the current Python version into `requires-python` (e.g. `>=3.12.3`), which is usually more restrictive than you need — change it to `>=3.11` manually. - A script in a directory that has a `pyproject.toml` is treated as a project script by default; pass the explicit `--script` flag to override: `uv run --script script.py`. - No lockfile by default — for reproducibility, run `uv lock --script script.py` to pin the dep graph.
**Sources:** [uv Scripts guide — docs.astral.sh](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/guides/scripts/) · [Share Python Scripts Like a Pro: uv and PEP 723 — thisdavej.com](https://thisdavej.com/share-python-scripts-like-a-pro-uv-and-pep-723-for-easy-deployment/) · [How to write a self-contained script — pydevtools.com](https://pydevtools.com/handbook/how-to/how-to-write-a-self-contained-script/)

item.title: Your OpenAI SDK Already Works Against Together AI's Open-Model Catalog — Swap base_url and a Model ID, Keep Everything Else
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Together AI serves 200+ open models via an OpenAI-compatible API. Set base_url to https://api.together.xyz/v1 and swap the model ID to call Llama, Qwen, or Mistral with existing SDK code.
item.content:encoded:
**What you'll be able to do after this:** call Llama 3.1, Qwen3, Mistral, and other open-weight models using your existing OpenAI Python client by changing one URL and one model string — no new SDK, no new abstractions.
**Three things to know first:** 1. Together's serverless tier is billed per token and ready instantly — but not every catalog model is available serverless. Check the model list before building on an ID. 2. Dedicated endpoints give you a reserved slot billed per minute of hosting whether or not you call them — useful under sustained high-concurrency load, costly for low-traffic experiments. 3. Together's API key is separate from OpenAI's. Store it as `TOGETHER_API_KEY`; don't reuse the same env variable.
## Setup
```bash pip install openai export TOGETHER_API_KEY="your-key-here" ```
## The one-line change
```python import os from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI( api_key=os.environ["TOGETHER_API_KEY"], base_url="https://api.together.xyz/v1", )
response = client.chat.completions.create( model="meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-Turbo", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain vector indexing in one paragraph."}], ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) ```
The entire `openai.OpenAI()` surface — streaming, tool calls, async client, LangChain's `ChatOpenAI` wrapper — works unchanged against Together's endpoint. Swap `base_url` at the client level and every call routes there.
## Together vs OpenRouter vs Fireworks — when to reach for which
- **Together:** fixed per-token pricing, 200+ open-model catalog, fine-tuning API built in (train a LoRA adapter, deploy it, serve it — all in one platform) - **OpenRouter:** routes across multiple providers for best price or availability; useful when you need provider-level failover or want to compare outputs across hosts - **Fireworks:** optimized for structured generation and JSON mode at high throughput; tends to win on latency for those specific workloads
## Limits
Not every model in the catalog is serverless-callable — some require a dedicated endpoint. Rate limits on the serverless tier can be restrictive at high concurrency; request an increase through the Together dashboard. Dedicated endpoints are billed per minute of active hosting, so tear them down when not in use. Model IDs in the catalog change over time — pin the full string rather than inferring it programmatically.
