item.title: Anthropic Reports New Distillation Defenses — If You Generate Synthetic Training Data From Claude, Know the Line
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Anthropic published new distillation defenses Oct 12, reporting 90-99% reduction in extractable reasoning data. The line for engineers: task-specific labeled data generation is not what these defenses target.
item.content:encoded:
**Anthropic published new distillation defenses October 12; if you generate synthetic training data from Claude at scale, know which patterns trigger the classifiers — and which don't.**
[Anthropic's new research post](https://anthropic.com/research/distillation-defenses) reports model- and API-level safeguards that reduce the reasoning data distillation campaigns can extract by roughly 90–99%, per Anthropic's own early measurements. Context: Anthropic's September 2026 threat report ([Betterstack summary](https://betterstack.com/community/guides/ai/anthropic-threat-report-2026/)) described seven AI labs running campaigns totaling 190 million exchanges — Alibaba's lab alone contributing 151 million — characterized as wholesale attempts to reproduce Claude's general-purpose reasoning in a smaller model.
The defenses target coordinated multi-account extraction, chain-of-thought elicitation at volume, and patterns consistent with training a competing general model. They do not target standard API use.
**The engineering line:** generating task-specific labeled data — classification labels, Q&A pairs, structured outputs for your own downstream fine-tune — is not what these defenses are for, as long as you use a single legitimate account and are not trying to replicate Claude's general capabilities. Anthropic's usage policy prohibits training a competing general model from Claude outputs; task-specific fine-tuning for your own application is a different thing.
**Why it matters:** If you scale up a synthetic data pipeline against the Claude API, the new behavioral classifiers will be watching. Keep volume proportionate to the task, stay on one account, and document the purpose.
**Sources:** [Strengthening our defenses against distillation attacks — Anthropic](https://anthropic.com/research/distillation-defenses) · [Anthropic September 2026 Threat Report — Betterstack](https://betterstack.com/community/guides/ai/anthropic-threat-report-2026/)

item.title: Describe Layout to Claude Design, Describe Behavior to Claude Code — The Spec Split That Keeps the Handoff Clean
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Mixing visual and behavioral requirements in one prompt drops the behavior silently. Split into a layout spec for Claude Design and a behavior spec for Claude Code.
item.content:encoded:
**Mixing visual and behavioral requirements in a single Claude Design prompt drops the behavior silently — the artboard generates static layout, not interaction logic. Split your spec before you prompt.**
The typical failure: "a settings panel with real-time toggle that saves to the API on change" generates the visual panel accurately. The save-on-change requirement is silently discarded — Claude Design has nowhere to put it. Claude Code then inherits a component that looks right but must work around the visual structure to add the behavior you described.
The fix is two documents, not one.
**What Claude Design responds to**
Visual and structural language: layout type (grid, flex), spacing values, typography scale, color tokens, component slots, and named aesthetic directions. Prompts that work:
- "Two-column section: 200px fixed label column, right column with a toggle switch, 16px row gaps" - "Material-like density — small type, no wasted whitespace, controls flush to their labels" - "Stacks to single column below 480px; toggle stays right-aligned at all widths"
It also responds to explicit breakpoint behavior and named components ("uses our existing Badge and Icon components"). What it cannot do: generate handlers, API calls, form validation, conditional state, transitions, or animation timing.
**What goes to Claude Code**
Everything that happens over time. Write a separate requirements doc using the class names or slot IDs Claude Design assigned:
> The `toggle-row` component calls `PATCH /api/settings/:key` on change; on success it shows a 200ms green flash on the row's status indicator; on failure it reverts the toggle and sets `aria-invalid` on it.
This spec references the component by name from the design output, so Claude Code knows exactly where to wire the behavior.
**The verification step**
After exporting the bundle, scan the output for hardcoded event listeners or conditional display logic. Delete anything you find — it represents the design tool attempting to satisfy a behavioral prompt it cannot fully execute, and it will conflict with Claude Code's implementation. Move those requirements explicitly into your Claude Code spec.
**Limit**
Splitting the spec takes 15–20 minutes upfront. It pays off on features with five or more components or multiple interaction states. For a two-component prototype you'll iterate and discard, a combined prompt is faster. The split matters at the start of implementation work, not during early exploration.
**Sources:** [Get started with Claude Design — Anthropic Support](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/14604416-get-started-with-claude-design) · [Anthropic overhauled Claude Design — The New Stack](https://thenewstack.io/anthropic-claude-design-overhaul/) · [Claude Design Review — Builder.io](https://www.builder.io/blog/claude-design)

item.title: Your Browser Test Agent Can Now Profile Memory and Check PWA Behavior — Chrome DevTools MCP October Additions
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Chrome 153 adds heap-snapshot querying, PWA lifecycle tools, and a JS-eval kill switch to the DevTools MCP server. Wire them into your Claude Code test sessions.
item.content:encoded:
**Chrome 153 adds heap-snapshot querying, PWA lifecycle automation, and a JS-eval kill switch to the DevTools MCP server — your Claude Code test sessions pick them up on a Chrome restart.**
The Chrome DevTools MCP server — which lets Claude Code and other agents drive a browser session via the Model Context Protocol — gained three new tool clusters in the October 2026 Chrome release.
**Heap snapshot querying.** The DevTools memory profiler tools are now exposed through the MCP interface. Use this in a test session to check for listener or closure leaks: ask Claude Code to count object allocations for a specific class before and after a component mount/unmount cycle. Previously this required custom Playwright `evaluate()` calls and a separate profiling harness.
**PWA lifecycle automation.** New tools trigger the browser's install prompt, verify service worker registration, test offline fallback behavior, and confirm manifest parsing — the three steps that validate a PWA works as intended. These are the same operations you run manually in the browser's Application panel, now available to test agents without bespoke Playwright scripts.
**`--no-javascript-evaluation` flag.** Pass this when starting the Chrome session to prevent the MCP server from executing JavaScript in the page context. Use it when the page enforces a strict `script-src` CSP, or when you want to guarantee the test agent only reads DOM state without running code in the page.
**How to connect.** Launch Chrome 153+ with `--remote-debugging-port=9222` and add the DevTools MCP server to your session's `.mcp.json`. The new tools register automatically once Chrome is updated — no additional configuration changes needed.
**Limit.** Chrome 153 is on the Canary/Dev channel in October 2026; stable channel release typically follows 6–8 weeks later. MCP tool schemas may change before stable rollout — pin the Chrome version in CI environments building on these APIs. Independent practitioner write-ups are limited since this just shipped.
**Sources:** [New in Chrome DevTools October 2026 — Chrome Developers](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/new-in-devtools-october-2026)

item.title: Three Sketches Before One Commit: Use Claude Design to Explore Multiple UI Directions Before Your Claude Code Session Starts
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Prompt Claude Design for two or three distinct UI approaches, pick one, export the bundle — your Claude Code session then starts from a real spec instead of a verbal description.
item.content:encoded:
**Prompt Claude Design for alternatives, evaluate them against your codebase constraints, then hand Claude Code the winner as a structured bundle — not a verbal description.**
The default Claude Code flow — "make a dashboard for X" — gives you a spec the model wrote for itself based on your description. It's usually plausible, but the model is deciding what the UI should look like, not you. This workflow reverses that. You use Claude Design to generate the alternatives, you pick the one that fits your existing system, and Claude Code implements to the spec you chose.
**Step 1: ask for directions, not a single design**
Instead of describing the result you want, describe the decision you're trying to make:
``` Give me three different approaches to a notification panel: one that's minimal (inbox-style, no icons, density-first), one that's card-based (each notification gets a card with an action button), one that's sidebar-persistent (always visible, collapsible). Dark background, accent #3b82f6. Keep component shapes simple. ```
Claude Design produces each approach as a separate artifact. You now have three things to evaluate, not three things to imagine.
**Step 2: evaluate against your actual constraints**
Before you export anything, run three checks on each direction:
- Does it use primitives you already have (Button, Badge, Icon, Card)? - Does it work in the contexts where it will actually appear (mobile drawer, embedded panel, desktop sidebar)? - Does anything require a token or type scale not in your existing design system?
The direction that passes all three costs the least to implement. Claude Code can close small gaps — a missing variant, a spacing adjustment — but it's poor at inventing missing foundation components mid-session.
**Step 3: export and hand off to Claude Code**
Export the chosen direction. The bundle contains a machine-readable component structure, the design tokens it references, and the layout hierarchy. Open Claude Code:
``` Implement the notification panel from ./notification-panel-spec.zip. Use our existing Button, Badge, and Icon components from app/components/. Don't invent new token names — map to our existing spacing and color scale in app/lib/theme.ts. ```
Claude Code implements to the spec rather than improvising. If the result needs adjustment, make it in the editor — don't round-trip back to the design tool for pixel-level changes, only for direction-level ones.
**Where this breaks down:** Claude Design is research preview. Vague prompts produce generic-looking output. The more specific your Step 1 constraints (named components, explicit contexts, real token values), the less cleanup you need in Step 3. Don't expect a generated spec to be production-ready — expect it to be a better starting point than a blank file or a verbal brief.

item.title: Your Claude Code Session Compacts Itself at 80% — Run /compact Early With a Focus Instruction to Keep What Actually Matters
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Claude Code auto-compacts at ~80% context utilization. Add a focus instruction to /compact so the summary preserves your task state, not whatever a generic summarizer picks.
item.content:encoded:
**Run `/compact` manually before the 80% warning with a focus instruction — the text you add is kept verbatim in the compacted summary, so Claude preserves task state the generic auto-compact would lose.**
Claude Code auto-compacts the conversation at roughly 80% context utilization (around 160,000 tokens in a 200K window). This keeps the session alive across a long task, but the default compaction is generic: it optimizes for overall coverage, not for the twelve specific files you've been editing, the failing test names you were mid-way through fixing, or the reason you decided not to touch `packages/auth/`.
The `/compact` command lets you run compaction on your terms:
``` /compact keep: the full list of modified files, the names of failing tests in packages/api/__tests__/, and the current plan to refactor SessionManager before AuthMiddleware ```
Claude includes your instruction text verbatim in the compacted summary. Without a focus instruction, you're relying on the same generic summarizer the auto-compact uses.
**Three useful patterns:**
**1. End-of-phase compaction.** Before shifting from reading/exploring to writing/testing:
``` /compact keep: I've read the auth module in packages/auth/, the key invariant is X, the files I need to edit are token.ts and middleware.ts, and I haven't touched the DB layer yet ```
**2. Milestone summary.** After a feature is done, before starting the next:
``` /compact keep: notification panel is done (app/components/NotificationPanel.tsx, tests pass), next task is to wire it into the header in app/layout.tsx ```
This also functions as a session handoff note — the compacted summary is what you'd resume from.
**3. Bug-fix context.** When the reproduce path is the key thing to preserve:
``` /compact keep: the bug is in auth/token.ts line 147 — JWT refresh silently swallows the expiry error when the clock is skewed. Reproduce: set system clock back 5 min, sign in, refresh. The test I wrote is in __tests__/token.test.ts. ```
**When to run it:** at natural pauses — after finishing a sub-task, before switching modes. Running at 90% after auto-compaction may have already fired is too late.
**One real limit:** `/compact` resets the scroll-back history. Earlier messages are replaced by the summary and can't be retrieved. Keep a running `notes.md` in your project for anything you'll want to reference again, because the compacted context is a lossy one-way door.
**Sources:** [morphllm.com — Claude Code /compact guide](https://morphllm.com/claude-code-compact) · [Claude Code auto-compact behavior — morphllm.com](https://www.morphllm.com/claude-code-auto-compact) · [Claude Code context management — sfeir.com](https://institute.sfeir.com/en/claude-code/claude-code-context-management/cheatsheet/)

item.title: FAISS Has No Native Persistence and pgvector Needs Postgres — Chroma's PersistentClient Gives You a Local Vector Store in One pip install
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: chromadb.PersistentClient(path="./db") writes an embedded vector store to a directory — no server, no schema migration. Good for local RAG prototypes before committing to hosted infrastructure.
item.content:encoded:
**What you'll be able to do after this:** run a local vector similarity search that survives process restarts — a portable RAG prototype that works without a cloud account or a running server, and migrates to pgvector or Qdrant when you're ready to scale.
The vector store landscape has three natural tiers:
| Tier | Example | Persistence | Server? | |---|---|---|---| | In-process, no persistence | FAISS | No native disk write | No | | Embedded, persistent | **Chroma** | Directory on disk | No | | Server-backed | pgvector, Qdrant | Database/cluster | Yes |
Chroma sits in the middle. Use it when you need more than FAISS's rebuild-every-restart but aren't ready to spin up Postgres or a vector DB server for a prototype.
**Setup:**
```python pip install chromadb ```
```python import chromadb
# Data persists to ./my_rag_db across process restarts client = chromadb.PersistentClient(path="./my_rag_db")
# get_or_create_collection is idempotent — safe to call on every startup collection = client.get_or_create_collection(name="docs") ```
The default embedding function uses `sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2` locally (downloaded on first use). No API key required.
**Adding documents:**
```python collection.add( documents=[ "Chroma embeds text automatically using the collection's embedding function.", "FAISS requires you to supply pre-computed embeddings as numpy arrays.", "pgvector stores vectors in a Postgres column; you need the pg_vector extension." ], ids=["doc-1", "doc-2", "doc-3"] # must be unique strings ) ```
Duplicate IDs raise an error. Use `collection.upsert(...)` when updating existing documents.
**Querying:**
```python results = collection.query( query_texts=["how does Chroma handle embeddings?"], n_results=2 ) # results["documents"][0] — matched doc strings # results["distances"][0] — L2 or cosine distances (lower = closer) # results["ids"][0] — matched ids ```
**Switching to a better embedding model:**
Pass a custom `embedding_function` at creation time and again every time you call `get_or_create_collection` — Chroma verifies it matches what the collection was created with:
```python from chromadb.utils.embedding_functions import HuggingFaceEmbeddingFunction
hf_ef = HuggingFaceEmbeddingFunction( api_key="YOUR_HF_TOKEN", model_name="sentence-transformers/all-mpnet-base-v2" ) collection = client.get_or_create_collection(name="docs", embedding_function=hf_ef) ```
**One real limit:** Chroma is a single-process embedded database — not designed for concurrent writes from multiple processes or for collections above a few million documents. When you hit either constraint, migrate to Qdrant (local Docker) or pgvector (Postgres + `CREATE EXTENSION vector`). The query API is similar enough that the swap costs one abstraction layer, not a rewrite.
**Sources:** [Chroma docs — PersistentClient](https://docs.trychroma.com/guides) · [Chroma docs — create/get/delete collections](https://docs.trychroma.com/docs/collections/create-get-delete) · [DataCamp Chroma tutorial](https://www.datacamp.com/tutorial/chromadb-tutorial-step-by-step-guide)

item.title: Your Claude Code Overnight Run Will Exhaust Its WebSearch Budget Unless You Tune the Refill Rate First
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Claude Code now refills its WebSearch budget at 100 calls/hour instead of ending at a hard 200-call wall. Three env vars control the limits before you kick off a long autonomous run.
item.content:encoded:
**Claude Code's WebSearch budget is now a leaky bucket, not a wall — but only if you let it refill.**
As of Claude Code v2.1.292 (October 6), the per-session WebSearch limit changed from a hard 200-call ceiling to a **token-bucket pattern**: the budget refills at 100 calls per hour. For an overnight research sweep, codebase audit, or batch document processing run, that means search calls won't suddenly fail at call 201 — as long as your throughput stays within the hourly refill rate.
**Three settings to review before a long autonomous run:**
`CLAUDE_CODE_WEB_SEARCH_REFILLS_PER_HOUR` (default: `100`) Controls how quickly the budget refills. Set to `0` to turn off refilling and revert to a predictable hard cap — useful in CI where you want deterministic resource usage.
`CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS` (default: `20`) Maximum subagents running simultaneously. Fan-out workflows that spawn many parallel workers may need this raised; sequential pipelines benefit from keeping it low to make session behavior easier to debug.
`CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH` (default: `3`) Maximum nesting depth: orchestrator (depth 1) → worker (depth 2) → sub-worker (depth 3). Raising past 3 increases coordination complexity quickly; behavior beyond 3 levels is less tested in production.
**For network-sensitive production deployments**, add `"sandbox.network.strictAllowlist": true` to `.claude/settings.json`. Sandboxed shell commands will then be denied for any host not on the `allowedDomains` list, rather than prompting (requires v2.1.219+). It fails closed, so test your `allowedDomains` list in staging before enabling it in production.
**One real limit:** The refill applies to interactive terminal sessions, but headless runs (`claude -p`) and subagent-spawned searches count against the same session counter. A large fan-out of parallel subagents each doing web searches can exhaust the bucket faster than it refills. For those workloads, raising `CLAUDE_CODE_WEB_SEARCH_REFILLS_PER_HOUR` above 100 — or switching subagents to use curated document retrieval instead of open web search — is the more effective control.
**Sources:** [Claude Code settings reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference) · [Claude Code changelog](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog) · [Sandboxing docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing) · [RFC 2697 — Token Bucket algorithm (IETF)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2697)

item.title: Your Fine-Tune Trains 1% of the Model's Parameters — LoRA Splits Each Target Weight Into Two Low-Rank Matrices and Trains Only Those
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: LoRA freezes pretrained weights and trains only two low-rank matrices per layer. Pick rank, alpha, and target_modules; five lines of PEFT code apply it to any transformer.
item.content:encoded:
**What you'll be able to do after this:** freeze a pretrained model, attach trainable low-rank adapter matrices with five lines of PEFT code, and merge them back into the base model for deployment with no inference overhead.
A full fine-tune updates every weight in the model. At 7B parameters that is manageable on a consumer GPU; at 70B it requires a server cluster. LoRA's observation is that the **weight update** during fine-tuning — the difference between fine-tuned and pretrained weights — is low-rank in practice. Instead of updating ΔW directly, you approximate it as two small matrices:
``` ΔW ≈ B × A, where A ∈ ℝ^(r×d), B ∈ ℝ^(d×r), r ≪ d ```
For a 4096×4096 attention projection with r=8: two matrices of 8×4096 — 65,536 trainable parameters instead of 16.7M. The [Hu et al. LoRA paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685) reports a ~10,000× reduction in trainable parameters for GPT-3-scale models, with **zero added inference latency** because the adapter can be merged back into the base weights after training.
**Three numbers you choose:**
| Setting | What it controls | |---|---| | `r` (rank) | Dimensionality of the low-rank space. 4–8 for simple adaptation; 16–64 for complex tasks or larger models | | `lora_alpha` | Scaling factor for the LoRA contribution (equivalent to `lora_alpha / r`). Start at 2× `r` as a rule of thumb | | `target_modules` | Which weight matrices to adapt. `"all-linear"` is the safe default; targeting only `q_proj, v_proj` is lighter but may miss behavior |
**Apply it in five lines:**
```python from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model
config = LoraConfig(r=8, lora_alpha=16, target_modules="all-linear", lora_dropout=0.05) model = get_peft_model(base_model, config) model.print_trainable_parameters() # trainable params: 3,407,872 || all params: 6,742,609,920 || trainable%: 0.051 ```
Train with any standard PyTorch loop or TRL's `SFTTrainer`. After training, merge the adapter for zero-overhead inference:
```python merged = model.merge_and_unload() # adapter weights folded in; no separate overhead at inference ```
**Limits:** LoRA works well for behavioral adaptation — instruction-following, domain vocabulary, style — because those updates are genuinely low-rank. Tasks that require memorizing factual knowledge not in the base model need more data or a higher `r`; at high enough `r` you lose most of the memory benefit over full fine-tuning. Also, `merge_and_unload()` is permanent: the resulting checkpoint is a new base model, not an adapter you can remove.
The [HuggingFace LLM Course chapter on LoRA](https://huggingface.co/learn/llm-course/chapter11/4) walks through the full training loop including `SFTTrainer` configuration and a worked Llama fine-tune example. The companion [smol-course unit](https://huggingface.co/learn/smol-course/unit1/3a) covers hotswapping multiple adapters — loading adapter A, switching to adapter B without reloading the base model — which is useful when you maintain specialized variants of the same base.
**Sources:** [HuggingFace LLM Course — LoRA (chapter 11/4)](https://huggingface.co/learn/llm-course/chapter11/4) · [PEFT docs — LoRA reference](https://huggingface.co/docs/peft/v0.20.0/package_reference/lora) · [HuggingFace smol-course — LoRA and PEFT](https://huggingface.co/learn/smol-course/unit1/3a) · [Hu et al. LoRA paper (arxiv)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685)

item.title: Your Postgres Database Is Already a Vector Store — Enable pgvector and You Are One CREATE INDEX Away from Semantic Search
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: pgvector adds a vector column type and cosine similarity operators to Postgres. Supabase's vecs Python client manages collections, upserts embeddings, and queries them in four lines — with a free Colab to run live.
item.content:encoded:
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Add durable, queryable vector storage to any Postgres database — including your existing Supabase project — without a separate vector database service.
**Three things to understand**
1. **pgvector extends Postgres with a `vector` column type and similarity operators.** `<=>` is cosine distance; `<->` is Euclidean. Add a `CREATE INDEX … USING hnsw` to turn brute-force scans into approximate nearest-neighbor queries that stay fast past a million rows.
2. **Supabase enables it with one dashboard click.** Database → Extensions → search "vector" → enable. From there, `CREATE TABLE docs (id bigserial primary key, embedding vector(384));` is all the schema you need.
3. **The `vecs` Python client wraps collections, upsert, and query.** It manages the table schema behind a simple API, auto-creates an HNSW index on first `create_index()` call, and returns matched records with metadata filters.
**Steps (Supabase + vecs)**
Install: ```bash pip install vecs sentence-transformers ```
Connect and create a collection: ```python import vecs, os
# get the connection URI from Supabase → Settings → Database → Connection string # use the POOLER string (port 6543) if running from Colab — Colab blocks IPv6 vx = vecs.create_client(os.environ["SUPABASE_DB_URL"]) docs = vx.get_or_create_collection(name="docs", dimension=384) ```
Upsert embeddings: ```python from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2") # 384-dim, runs on CPU
records = [ ("doc-1", model.encode("pgvector adds cosine similarity to Postgres").tolist(), {"source": "intro"}), ("doc-2", model.encode("HNSW index: built incrementally, 2-5x more RAM than IVFFlat").tolist(), {"source": "docs"}), ] docs.upsert(records=records) docs.create_index() # builds HNSW; idempotent if called twice ```
Query: ```python query_vec = model.encode("How does Postgres handle vector search?").tolist()
results = docs.query( data=query_vec, limit=3, filters={"source": {"$eq": "docs"}}, # metadata filter applied pre-scan include_metadata=True, ) # → [("doc-2", 0.08, {"source": "docs"}), ...] ```
**Run this in 15 minutes:** Supabase's [Hello World Colab notebook](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/ai/quickstarts/hello-world) walks through the full workflow against a free Supabase project — no local setup required.
**Why pgvector over an in-process store**
FAISS (covered [earlier in this series](https://cloudcodetree.com/ai-news/2026-10-05-04-faiss-ivf-hnsw-index-types-ann-in-process)) disappears on process exit and rebuilds on restart. pgvector lives in Postgres: vectors survive reboots, share a connection pool with your application data, and sit behind your existing row-level security and backups. The tradeoff is that managed Postgres adds network overhead — for a batch job that only ever runs locally, an in-process store is faster.
**Limits worth knowing**
- **Filtered queries can return fewer rows than `limit`.** The HNSW index scans a neighborhood and stops when it has enough candidates; a tight metadata filter may leave fewer qualifying rows than requested. Increase `hnsw.ef_search` (default 40) when high recall matters more than latency. - **2,000-dimension cap.** Postgres/pgvector supports up to 2,000 dimensions per vector. Models that produce ≥ 3,072-dim vectors (OpenAI's text-embedding-3-large at full resolution, for example) need PCA or MRL reduction before storage. - **IVFFlat requires data first.** Unlike HNSW, IVFFlat needs rows present at index-creation time to find cluster centers. Build it after you've loaded a representative sample, not on an empty table.
**Sources:** [pgvector: Embeddings and vector similarity — Supabase Docs](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/extensions/pgvector) · [Vecs Python client — Supabase Docs](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/ai/vecs-python-client) · [Hello World Colab — Supabase AI Quickstarts](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/ai/quickstarts/hello-world) · [HNSW vs IVFFlat: index types in PostgresML](https://postgresml.org/blog/hnsw-vs-ivfflat-vector-indexes-in-postgresml)

item.title: Your Parallel Subagents Don't All Need the Same Reasoning Budget — The Agent Tool's `effort` Field Right-Sizes Thinking Intensity Across a Workflow
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Claude Code's new Agent tool effort field lets you set reasoning intensity per subagent — low for parallel searches, high for synthesis — without changing the main session.
item.content:encoded:
**Pass `effort: "low"` to parallel searchers and `effort: "high"` to the synthesis step — each subagent runs at its natural reasoning depth without changing the main session's settings.**
A subagent launched with the Agent tool runs at the session's default effort level, which is right for hard analysis but wasteful for well-defined tasks like scanning files, summarizing a doc, or fetching known facts. Claude Code added an `effort` field to the Agent tool in v2.1.292 (October 6, 2026), so you can set reasoning intensity per launch.
**Fan-out with tiered effort** (in a Workflow script):
```javascript // Three parallel searches at low effort const findings = await parallel([ () => agent("Find all TODOs in src/", { effort: "low", label: "search-todos" }), () => agent("List uses of deprecated APIs", { effort: "low", label: "search-deprecated" }), () => agent("Check package.json for outdated deps", { effort: "low", label: "check-deps" }), ])
// One synthesis agent at high effort const report = await agent( "Synthesize these into a prioritized action plan: " + JSON.stringify(findings), { effort: "high", label: "synthesize" } ) ```
The same field works in a custom subagent definition's YAML frontmatter:
```yaml --- model: inherit effort: low --- ```
**Resolution order:** per-call `effort` overrides the definition's frontmatter, which overrides the session's effort level. Neither can override the `CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL` environment variable — if your CI sets that env var, per-call overrides won't pierce it. Run `/tasks` to see the effort level applied to each active subagent alongside its model, which is the fastest way to confirm settings are working as expected.
**Limits:** - `effort` controls thinking intensity only; it does not change the model (use `model: "haiku"` for that) - "low" effort may skip subtle edge cases or require more precise task wording — best for well-defined, verifiable queries - Available effort levels may be constrained by your organization's model allowlist; check before writing effort levels into CI automation
**Sources:** [Claude Code changelog](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog), [Claude Code subagents](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code/sub-agents), [HumanLayer — sub-agent models and effort](https://docs.humanlayer.com/reference/subagent-models)

item.title: Claude Code Gains Plugin-Modifiable Core Behavior, a Watchdog Side Agent, and Haiku 5.5 as Its Default Model
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Claude Code v2.1.287-293: Mods let plugins intercept and rewrite tool calls; You Should Know adds an opt-in watchdog agent; Haiku 5.5 with 1M context is now the default model.
item.content:encoded:
**Mods let plugins intercept and rewrite tool calls; You Should Know adds an opt-in watchdog side agent; Haiku 5.5 (1M context) is the new default — three Claude Code updates from October 1–7.**
**Claude Mods (v2.1.287, October 1)** extends the plugin system beyond tool-adding: a mod can draw a pane above the prompt, install a slash command that runs immediately, and intercept or rewrite a tool call before Claude executes it. Mods are JavaScript or TypeScript functions that run inside Claude Code with your local permissions. They are not sandboxed.
The built-in **"You Should Know" mod** (`cc-plugin-you-should-know@builtin`) is the first example of the pattern: a side agent watches your session and surfaces things you or Claude might miss, displayed above the prompt. Disabled by default; requires telemetry on:
``` /plugin enable cc-plugin-you-should-know@builtin ```
**Haiku 5.5 as default (v2.1.293, October 7):** Claude Code now uses Haiku 5.5 as its default model, which carries a 1M-token context window. Coding tasks that previously required splitting across sessions can now run in a single context window. Check which model your session uses with `/model`.
**Why it matters:** Mods open a new class of Claude Code tooling — plugins that sit between Claude and the tools it calls, not just alongside them. The 1M default context is a practical improvement for any multi-file or large-codebase task.
**Limits:** Mods run unsandboxed — review what a mod does before installing from a marketplace. You Should Know adds latency (a side agent runs on every turn). Your organization's model allowlist may not include Haiku 5.5; verify with `/model` before relying on it.
**Why it matters for this reader:** the Mods architecture makes pre-tool-call hooks first-class — you can now build a mod that checks a destructive operation against your policy before Claude runs it.
**Sources:** [Claude Code changelog](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog), [Claude Code Mods overview — havoptic.com](https://www.havoptic.com/releases/claude-code/2026/10)

item.title: Your Agent Executes Irreversible Steps Without Asking — LangGraph's `interrupt()` Freezes the Graph, Persists State, and Resumes on Your Signal
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: LangGraph's interrupt() pauses a graph mid-node, checkpoints all state, and returns a payload to your caller. Command(resume=...) picks up exactly where it stopped — no restart needed.
item.content:encoded:
**`interrupt()` freezes a LangGraph node mid-run, persists the graph state automatically, and resumes via `Command(resume=...)` exactly where it stopped — no restart, no lost context.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** add an approval gate to any node in a LangGraph agent so risky operations — file writes, external API calls, emails — pause and wait for explicit confirmation before executing.
**Three things to know first:**
1. `interrupt(payload)` raises inside a node, checkpointing the full graph state; your caller receives `payload` and can show it to a human 2. `Command(resume=response)` restarts from the interrupted node — `interrupt()` returns `response`, so the node can branch on it 3. A checkpointer is required; without one, `interrupt()` raises a `ValueError`. Use `MemorySaver` for dev, `PostgresSaver` for production
**Working example:**
```python from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, MessagesState from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver from langgraph.types import interrupt, Command
def review_before_send(state: MessagesState) -> MessagesState: draft = state["messages"][-1].content # Pause and hand the draft to a human decision = interrupt({"draft": draft, "action": "approve_or_edit"}) if decision.get("action") == "edit": return {"messages": [{"role": "assistant", "content": decision["text"]}]} return state # approved, continue as-is
builder = StateGraph(MessagesState) builder.add_node("review", review_before_send) # ... wire the rest of your graph graph = builder.compile(checkpointer=MemorySaver())
config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "draft-42"}}
# First invoke — runs until interrupt, returns the payload result = graph.invoke({"messages": [...]}, config) # result["__interrupt__"][0].value == {"draft": "...", "action": "approve_or_edit"}
# Human reviews; resume the graph final = graph.invoke(Command(resume={"action": "approve"}), config) ```
**In production:** replace `MemorySaver` with `AsyncPostgresSaver` — the in-process saver loses state on server restart or across instances.
**Limits:** - LangGraph does not expire interrupted threads automatically; implement a TTL or cleanup job yourself - Any code before `interrupt()` in the same node re-runs on resume — make it idempotent or move side effects after the call - `MemorySaver` is per-process and per-session; use `AsyncPostgresSaver` for concurrent production workloads - The interrupt payload must be JSON-serializable
**Sources:** [LangGraph interrupts — official docs](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/interrupts), [Making it easier to build human-in-the-loop agents (LangChain blog)](https://blog.langchain.com/making-it-easier-to-build-human-in-the-loop-agents-with-interrupt), [Human-in-the-loop with LangGraph walkthrough](https://rentierdigital.xyz/blog/human-in-the-loop-langgraph)

item.title: Your GPU Server Runs a Model — vLLM Makes It an OpenAI-Compatible Endpoint Your Existing Client Code Can Already Call
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server --model serves any HuggingFace model as an OpenAI-compatible endpoint — change base_url and your existing client code routes to your self-hosted model unchanged.
item.content:encoded:
**Serve any HuggingFace model as an OpenAI-compatible API with three commands — then route your existing `openai.chat.completions.create()` calls to it by changing one line.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** host an open model on your own GPU, call it from any existing OpenAI-client code unchanged, and handle concurrent team requests through a single shared inference endpoint.
**Three-command quickstart** (requires a CUDA GPU; check the vLLM install docs for ROCm or CPU builds):
```bash pip install vllm python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server \ --model mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 \ --port 8000 ```
Then in your application, change one line:
```python from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1", api_key="not-used") response = client.chat.completions.create( model="mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize this PR diff: ..."}] ) ```
Every other call in your codebase stays the same. vLLM implements `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/completions`, and `/v1/embeddings` to spec.
**Three takeaways:** - **`base_url` is the only change.** Your application, tests, and tooling all route to the self-hosted model without further edits. - **Continuous batching vs. Ollama.** vLLM's PagedAttention and continuous batching handle multiple concurrent callers in a single GPU forward pass — Ollama serializes them. For a shared team endpoint or high-throughput batch jobs, the difference is significant. - **Multi-GPU tensor parallelism is a flag.** Add `--tensor-parallel-size 2` to split a model across two GPUs; the serving API is unchanged.
**Where vLLM does not replace Ollama:** local dev workstations, macOS (Metal), and situations where automatic quantization and model management matter more than throughput. Ollama bundles everything; vLLM requires a separate install, a CUDA GPU, and explicit model management.
**Limits:** the Assistants API, Batch API, and fine-tuning endpoints are not implemented — vLLM exposes only the three inference endpoints listed above. The model must fit in available VRAM; use tensor parallelism to split across multiple GPUs rather than spilling to system RAM.

item.title: Your LLM Eval Run Costs Twice as Much as It Should — The Anthropic Message Batches API Cuts Per-Token Cost 50% for Async Workloads
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: client.beta.messages.batches.create() submits up to 10,000 requests at half the real-time per-token cost — right for eval suites, bulk document processing, and CI test data generation.
item.content:encoded:
**`client.beta.messages.batches.create()` submits up to 10,000 requests at half the real-time per-token cost — the right tool for eval suites, bulk document processing, and CI test data generation that can wait minutes to hours for results.**
Any workload that is large, doesn't need an immediate response, and runs off the critical path qualifies: eval runs, bulk summarization, test-case generation, embedding preprocessing. Anthropic quotes a 50% reduction vs. standard input/output rates — verify it holds for your specific model and token mix before rearchitecting around it.
**The pattern in three steps:**
**1. Create the batch:** ```python import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic() batch = client.beta.messages.batches.create(requests=[ { "custom_id": f"eval-{i}", "params": { "model": "claude-sonnet-5-5", "max_tokens": 256, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}] } } for i, prompt in enumerate(eval_prompts) ]) print(batch.id) # msgbatch_... ```
**2. Poll until complete:** ```python import time while True: batch = client.beta.messages.batches.retrieve(batch.id) if batch.processing_status == "ended": break time.sleep(60) # batches take minutes to hours; don't poll faster ```
**3. Stream results:** ```python for result in client.beta.messages.batches.results(batch.id): if result.result.type == "succeeded": print(result.custom_id, result.result.message.content[0].text) else: print(result.custom_id, "failed:", result.result.error) ```
**Takeaways:** - Up to 10,000 requests per batch; results stream by `custom_id` when processing ends - Batches time out after 24 hours; any requests still processing at that point expire - No streaming within a batch request — each request returns a full response object
**Limits:** batches are not for latency-sensitive paths — processing takes minutes to hours, not seconds. Not all models support the Batches endpoint; check the model's feature page before assuming support. Error handling is per-request: a single malformed request fails silently in the results stream unless you explicitly check every result's `.result.type`. The 50% rate reduction is Anthropic's own figure; run a comparison on your actual workload before assuming it.

item.title: Anthropic OSS Scanner Lets Open-Source Maintainers Opt In to Free AI Vulnerability Scanning — With No Human Triage on Reports
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Anthropic launched OSS Scanner on Oct 8: open-source maintainers enroll via PR, get periodic scans from Claude Mythos at no cost — but reports skip human triage and may include false positives.
item.content:encoded:
**Anthropic launched OSS Scanner on October 8: open-source maintainers submit a PR to opt in to periodic vulnerability scans from Claude Mythos — reports arrive without human review, so treat them as unverified candidates.**
Anthropic released OSS Scanner as part of its Cyber Mission initiative. Enrollment is a pull request to the `anthropics/oss-scanner` repository adding a project config file and a Dockerfile; Anthropic approves based on criteria similar to Google's OSS-Fuzz (security impact, active maintenance, core-maintainer verification). Scans run periodically at no charge.
The key thing to understand before enrolling: reports are fully model-generated and delivered to maintainers **without human review or triage**. Anthropic cites a historical >92% true-positive rate — but that figure comes from its separate coordinated-disclosure track, where external firms verify findings before delivery. OSS Scanner skips that step, so the false-positive rate is unknown and likely higher. Expect noise.
For engineers who maintain open-source AI tooling — libraries other agents or developers depend on — the enrollment is worth evaluating if you have triage capacity. Without it, an unreviewed flood of candidate reports creates more work, not less.
**Why it matters:** Automated vuln scanning became free for open-source projects overnight. But the no-review format shifts triage responsibility to maintainers. If you run a high-visibility library and have the bandwidth to process candidate reports, opt in. If you don't, wait for the tooling to mature.
One constraint from the announcement: OSS Scanner is opt-in for a reason — projects must explicitly enroll. Anthropic is not scanning the broader ecosystem unilaterally.

item.title: Your RAG Pipeline Has No Tests — RAGAS Scores Faithfulness and Context Precision Without a Single Hand-Written Gold Answer
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: RAGAS evaluates faithfulness, answer relevancy, and context precision without gold-standard answers — using an LLM judge that reads question + context + generated answer together.
item.content:encoded:
**RAGAS scores faithfulness, answer relevancy, and context precision without ground-truth answers — an LLM judge reads question, retrieved context, and generated answer together, so you can run it in CI from day one.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Run four scored metrics on your RAG outputs, diagnose whether failures come from retrieval or generation, and gate any metric in CI without labeling a single correct answer.
Three of the four core RAGAS metrics are reference-free — they don't need a hand-written "correct" answer because a judge LLM reasons over what was retrieved and what was generated:
- **Faithfulness** — extracts atomic claims from the generated answer, checks each against the retrieved context, returns the fraction supported. A low score means the generator added things that aren't in the retrieved chunks. - **Answer relevancy** — generates a synthetic question from the answer, embeds both, and measures cosine similarity to the original question. High similarity means the answer addresses what was asked. - **Context precision** — are the relevant chunks ranked near the top of retrieval? A retriever that buries the right content at rank 15 scores low even if it eventually finds it. - **Context recall** — what fraction of the reference answer is covered by retrieved context? This one *does* require a ground-truth reference, so it's best for batch evaluation on a labeled test set.
```python pip install ragas datasets
from datasets import Dataset from ragas import evaluate from ragas.metrics import faithfulness, answer_relevancy, context_precision
data = { "question": ["What changed in the Anthropic 2026 usage policy?"], "answer": ["The policy extended restrictions on autonomous agents in high-risk sectors."], "contexts": [[ "Anthropic updated its usage policy in November 2026, extending restrictions " "on autonomous agents operating in critical infrastructure and high-risk sectors." ]], } ds = Dataset.from_dict(data) result = evaluate(ds, metrics=[faithfulness, answer_relevancy, context_precision]) print(result) # {'faithfulness': 0.92, 'answer_relevancy': 0.88, 'context_precision': 1.0} ```
**Diagnostic logic:** If faithfulness is low but context precision is high, retrieval is working — your generator is reaching past the context to add things not in it (tighten the system prompt or lower temperature). If faithfulness is high but context precision is low, the generator is doing its best with poorly ranked chunks — fix the retriever.
**Two real limits:** First, faithfulness measures grounding, not truth. An answer that faithfully paraphrases incorrect context scores perfectly — RAGAS cannot catch this. Second, RAGAS itself is an LLM judge, so evaluation quality depends on your judge model and costs tokens. Start with a 50–100-question sample before wiring it to every PR.
**Sources:** [RAGAS evaluation quickstart — docs.ragas.io](https://docs.ragas.io/en/latest/getstarted/evaluation.html) · [RAG eval tutorial with RAGAS — Contextual AI docs](https://docs.contextual.ai/examples/tutorial-rag-eval-ragas) · [RAGAS metrics complete guide — qaskills.sh](https://qaskills.sh/blog/ragas-rag-evaluation-metrics-complete-guide)
